etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-, polite prefix) + 皿(さら) (sara, “plate”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) + 祭り (matsuri, “festival”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 一(いち) (ichi) + 番(ばん) (-ban).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Dialectal variation of standard Japanese ichiban.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 一 (hito, “one”) + 番 (tsugai, “pair, couple, brace”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 番(つが)う (tsugau)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Inherited from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ap-. Further etymology uncertain. Theories of earliest origin include:
* Imitative of the upper and lower lips meeting
* Shortened from 二肖経 (フタアエフ futa aefu, two go-together)
* Shortened from アアフツ (aa futsu), the latter portion a variant of 二(ふた)つ (futatsu, “two”)
* Either 間(あい) (ai, “relation”) → 逢(あふ) (afu, “meeting”) → 会(あう) (au) or 逢(あふ) (afu) → 間(あい) (ai) → 会(あう) (au)
Various forms of あう (合, 会, 逢, 遭; “join; be together; meet”) are attested from the Middle Ages (c. 1185-1573). Compare 合(あ)う (au).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Most likely derived ultimately from a mimetic word はた (hata, adverb, referring to the sound of objects bumping together), in turn possibly cognate with 旗 (hata, “flag”, from the sound of a flag flapping) and 機 (hata, “a loom”, from the sound of the shuttle or the workings of the batten).
Compare also adverb はたはた (hatahata, “working diligently”), verb はためく (hatameku, “to flutter, flap, flicker, whip”).
First cited in the late 900s, with the sense of "to move one's body".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 冷蔵(れいぞう) (reizō, “refrigeration”) + 庫(こ) (-ko, “depository”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese いだす (idasu), the causative form of 出づ (idu) Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *intasu.
First cited to the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.

etymologies.text:
⟨mi₁nami₁⟩ → */mʲinamʲɨ/ → /minami/
From Old Japanese 南 (mi₁nami₁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/minami/ → /minːami/

/natu/ → /nat͡su/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *natu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 夏 (MC haeH). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
Also used in the Man'yōshū (759 CE) as 借音 (shakuon) kana for ⟨ge₁⟩.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 夏 (MC haeX).
The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 大學 (MC dajH haewk).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 太し (puto₁si).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Found in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. In turn from Proto-Japonic *tuyə. Cognate with Miyako 強 (tsū), Okinawan 強ーさん (chūsan).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Nihon Shoki, c. CE 720. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kƏpa.
Cognate with 怖い (kowai, “scary, frightening”), apparently from the sense of freezing from fright. Likely also cognate with other terms beginning with ko- and related to senses of hard, stiff, such as 凝る (koru, “to stiffen”), 凍ゆ (koyu, “to freeze, to become frozen”, classical) → modern 凍える (kogoeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 掛く (kaku), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Probably a compound of 間 (hi, “free time”, possibly related to 皹 (hibi, “chap of the skin”)) + 間 (ma, “space, interval”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of いと (ito, “interval”, obsolete) + 間 (ma, “space, interval”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *asa. Attested in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Historically, a day was split into two halves:
* Afternoon cycle: 朝(あさ) (asa) → 昼(ひる) (hiru) → 夕(ゆう) (yū)
* Evening cycle: 夕(ゆう)べ (yūbe) → 宵(よい) (yoi) → 夜(よ)中(なか) (yonaka) → 暁(あかつき) (akatsuki) → 朝(あした) (ashita)
While asa and ashita represent the same time period, asa was associated with beginning of the afternoon and ashita was associated with the end of the night. Both terms share an initial as- and are likely etymologically related.
Beyond Japonic, possibly related to Middle Korean 아ᄎᆞᆷ〮 (àchóm, “morning”) > Korean 아침 (achim). Alexander Vovin believes this is a Koreanic borrowing into Japanese, identifying Japanese つとめて (tsutomete) as the native Japonic root for "morning" (Vovin 2010, p. 224).
* However, つとめて (tsutomete) is not attested until the late 800s or early 900s, although root 夙(つと) (tsuto) as in 夙(つと)に (tsuto ni, “early in the morning”, adverb) appears in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Alternatively, may be cognate with adjective 浅(あさ)い (asai, “shallow; early”), verbs 浅(あ)せる (aseru, “to become shallow”) and 褪(あ)せる (aseru, “to fade, to become pale”).
* The concepts of "shallow" and "deep" are used in other respects relative to time, such as 夜更(よふ)かし (yofukashi, “staying up late into the night”) and 夜(よ)更(ふ)け (yofuke, “very late at night”), where the fuk- root in both terms is from 深(ふか)い (fukai, “deep; late, long-lasting”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Historically, a day was split into two halves:
* Afternoon cycle: 朝(あさ) (asa) → 昼(ひる) (hiru) → 夕(ゆう) (yū)
* Evening cycle: 夕(ゆう)べ (yūbe) → 宵(よい) (yoi) → 夜(よ)中(なか) (yonaka) → 暁(あかつき) (akatsuki) → 朝(あした) (ashita)
While asa and ashita represent the same time period, asa was associated with beginning of the afternoon and ashita was associated with the end of the night. Both terms share an initial as- and are likely etymologically related.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/teu/ → /t͡ɕeu/ → /t͡ɕoː/
The "morning" and "Korea" senses are from Middle Chinese 朝 (MC trjew).
The "imperial court", "dynasty", and "epoch" senses are from Middle Chinese 朝 (MC drjew), using the 漢(かん)音(おん) (kan'on, literally “Han sound”) reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 比ぶ entry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived as the transitive form of Old Japanese verb 決む (kimu, “to decide something, to conclude something; to be decided, to be concluded”).
The source verb kimu appears to follow a common pattern in Old Japanese verbs where the bare form is either transitive or intransitive, depending on context. This pattern persists in some modern verbs, such as つく (tsuku). Many of these Old Japanese verbs developed explicit transitive and intransitive forms, with one group adopting an -aru on the end for the intransitive (as the 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis or incomplete form”) ending in -a + the conjugating る (ru) as the basic spontaneous or passive verb ending), and an -eru on the end for the transitive (as the 已然形 (izenkei, “realis or potential form”) + the disappearing る (ru) as a generic verb ending).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From classical -na adjective 珍(めずら) (mezura) + しい (-shii, adjective-forming suffix).
Ultimately from Old Japanese verb 愛づ (medu, medzu), modern Japanese 愛でる (mederu, “to love; to admire, to appreciate”).
The meaning originally referred to something that was admirable or favorable, something that had value, as an extension of the underlying verb. This meaning is used in the Man'yōshū, dating to the mid-700s. This further extended to indicate something that was rare or unusual in ways that one would find notable or attractive, and this meaning was also already used in the Man'yōshū. Over time, the admirable sense weakened, and the rare sense became dominant.
Cognate with Northern Amami Ōshima 珍っさり (むぃずぃらっさり, mïzïrassari).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *siru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 結構 (MC ket kuwH). Appears in the 小右記 (Shōyūki, Ouki) of 1031, the diary of Fujiwara no Sanesuke.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Related to 倣(なら)う (narau, “to imitate”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Same word as 入(い)る (iru, “to enter”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 見す (misu), following 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First cited to the Man'yōshū, circa 759 CE.
Analyzable as 見 (mi, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)る (miru, “to see; to look at”)) + す (-su, causative suffix, corresponding to modern せる (-seru)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 足 (asi, “leg; foot”). In turn, appears to be derived from or related to Old Japanese 足 (a, “leg; foot”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: An irregular shift in conjugation from the verb 足(た)る (taru), which originally followed 四(よ)段(だん) (yodan, “quadrigrade”) conjugation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tika.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *asonpu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 過ぐ (sugu). First attested in the Kojiki of 712.
Likely cognate with 挿(す)げる (sugeru, “to pass a hole through something”), 直(す)ぐ (sugu, “straight; soon”, adverb).
Reconstructed as deriving from Proto-Japonic *sunk-oi-.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *təpə. Cognate with Miyako 遠 (とぅー, tū), Okinawan 遠(とぅー)さん (tūsan).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from a verbalization of na-, the 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 音(ね) (ne, “sound, voice”). Doublet of 泣く (naku, “to cry”).
